title: How to Buy a Business With $0 (ft. Codie Sanchez)
guest: Codie Sanchez, entrepreneur and investor who buys and builds 'boring' cash-flowing businesses (laundromats, car washes) and teaches acquisition deal-making
summary: The hosts explain entrepreneurship through acquisition: search funds (the MBA-flavored, Stanford-institutionalized model), roll-ups, and who should and should not buy a business. Codie Sanchez argues the idea that you need your own capital is a lie sold by Wall Street, lays out seller financing, sweat equity and expertise-to-equity as zero-cash paths, gives diligence rules, and shares tactical advice for women on negotiating, mirroring sellers, and communicating concisely.

ideas.idea: The fastest way to become a CEO is not starting a company but buying one: the third path of 'buy then build' takes an existing profitable business from one to two instead of zero to one.
ideas.detail: Most people think the only routes are grinding 15+ years up the corporate ladder or starting a startup and 'emotionally collapsing in a WeWork'. Acquiring a mature business means you inherit a very different set of problems than a founder creates, but you are an entrepreneur and CEO immediately.

ideas.idea: A search fund is 'fund my job search, but the job is CEO': investors fund a searcher's full-time hunt for a business and pre-negotiate the right of first refusal to fund the acquisition.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Targets are lower-middle-market SMBs, roughly a $5-30 million acquisition doing $5-50 million in revenue or $1-5 million in annual profit, where a new CEO can professionalize operations. The classic seller is a 70-year-old owner of a multimillion-dollar plumbing business with no succession plan.

ideas.idea: Searching is unglamorous, multi-year sales work where most owners say no, so searchers need stamina, endurance and emotional management.
ideas.detail: Jean interned in 2009 for two Stanford GSB grads running a search fund and saw that it is day-in, day-out research and cold outreach, like knocking on a house with no for-sale sign. Owners are emotionally attached after 20-40 years and can back out right before signing, diligence can reveal skeletons, the economic environment can shift, and you must also manage investors and a co-searcher relationship.

ideas.idea: The search fund was coined at Harvard Business School in 1984 but institutionalized and popularized at Stanford by Professor Irv Grousbeck, with classes and alumni investor groups built around it.
ideas.detail: Cherie recently had coffee with Grousbeck, who is in his 90s, still teaching, and recently sold the Boston Celtics with his family; he pushed her toward entrepreneurship with the line 'I don't fear failing, I fear the regret of never having tried.' The 1984 innovation was having investors fund the search itself to match ambitious MBAs with retiring owners lacking succession plans.

ideas.idea: Diligence on an acquisition must include culture: interview the owner's top five to ten lieutenants, and contract the owner to stay on through a transition period.
ideas.detail: Employees of a 10-100 person company may be excited about new management or resentful when a 'scrappy 28-year-old' replaces the founder, so you want the direct reports bought in before you buy.

ideas.idea: Buying a business is for people who like operating, leading teams and handling messy real-life situations; it is not for anyone who wants passive income, hates managing humans, or wants to work from Bali.
ideas.detail: You will be changing the printer cartridge and making decisions without a 47-page strategy deck; there is nothing passive about it.

ideas.idea: The belief that you need your own capital to buy a business is a lie that serves private equity and large corporations; the real gap is knowledge, not money.
ideas.detail: 60% of businesses sold involve some seller financing, and PE firms themselves use leveraged buyouts, i.e. other people's money, just as homebuyers use mortgages. Private equity is the most profitable asset class over any 10-year rolling period, and Sanchez has seen first-time buyers do deals for $0 and for $50 million.

ideas.idea: There are three legs of the stool for buying a business without cash: seller financing, sweat equity, and expertise-to-equity.
ideas.detail: Most small business owners are 65+, and more than 60% have no transition plan, so they will accept a share of future profits. Sweat equity means earning part or all of the business through work, like startup equity; expertise-to-equity means trading a specific skill such as marketing for a percentage of ownership.

ideas.idea: Startups are a bad deal for founders: most businesses never make money, the ones that do lose money for three to four years, and the average entrepreneur earns $46,000-$67,000 a year.
ideas.detail: VCs know only one in ten startups will make it, which is fine for the VC but not for the founder; you can often make more as an employee. Both Sanchez and Jean had a 'look down the hall' moment in finance (Jean at Goldman) realizing they did not want the corner-office life, and the best part of entrepreneurship is becoming unemployable.

ideas.idea: For a first acquisition, buy a boring, bond-like business so simple grandma understands it, with checks coming in for at least five years; never buy someone else's pain or a turnaround.
ideas.detail: Unprofitable businesses that have not figured it out are the 'ugly house on the nice block' and the surest way to lose money. Boring businesses do not grow like a hockey stick but keep paying if you take the right actions.

ideas.idea: Three diligence rules: make sure the seller is not lying too badly, make sure the P&L matches the tax return (and buy on the cheaper number if it does not), and make sure you are buying a business, not a job.
ideas.detail: Every owner lies a little, via inflated add-backs, understated hours, or asking you to pay for 'future potential'. Diligence is a lot of work but formulaic, and a business needs enough systems, processes and employees that you do not end up doing everything.

ideas.idea: A woman buying from an older male owner should mirror the seller, show intensity, and redirect the conversation to profits and employees rather than invoking 'the patriarchy'.
ideas.detail: When a seller said he could not present a woman in her 30s to his investors, Sanchez's move would be shock plus reframe: what matters is making more money and taking care of employees, which has nothing to do with gender. How you dress, talk and push back matters more for women; if a seller will never sell to you, move on to a 'perfect fit seller' where your background (for Sanchez, speaking Spanish with landscaping owners) is an advantage.

ideas.idea: The search fund is a terrible model for the searcher and an incredible model for the fund, which owns 50-70% of a company the searcher found, financed and runs.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Sanchez teaches people to buy businesses for under $1,000 a month while keeping all their economics, because she thinks it is unfair to own part of a business someone must run for life just for teaching them; Wall Street wants the arbitrage and leverage without the hard work.

ideas.idea: Never fall in love with something that cannot love you back: being willing to walk away from a deal makes you more likely to win it, and there is no 'last best deal'.
ideas.detail: Suzy Welch says there is no last best deal except the one you did and wish you had not; Warren Buffett says he never thinks about deals he missed, only the ones he did but should not have.

ideas.idea: Invest somebody else's first $500,000 rather than your own, and start with partial acquisitions instead of blowing up your whole life.
ideas.detail: A Goldman mentor told her the first $500K in deals is almost sure to be lost, so learn on someone else's dime; men have long done 'club deals' on the 19th hole and own pieces of friends' businesses. Learning how to do a deal is like the Matrix: even if you never buy, you will negotiate and evaluate roles and companies differently.

ideas.idea: Women should build deal-sharing group chats the way men do: proactively send investment opportunities to a list of women and normalize saying no.
ideas.detail: Sanchez's investor base has been 99% men who proactively asked to invest, so she now texts her deals to a list of women even though it felt uncomfortable. Her investment in Brett Adcock's Figure, now valued at $38 billion, came from a male friend sending the deal; she trades deals with Sophia Amoruso of Trust Fund VC. The hosts noticed at business school that men's group chats covered angel deals while women's did not.

ideas.idea: The best ROI is spelled YOU: investing in your own skills has unlimited upside while every other asset class is capped.
ideas.detail: For the next 90 days, learn as much as possible about money, ideally deal-making, via 'skill stacking' as Scott Adams describes; her $47 three-day virtual MSM Live event is her cheapest entry point. Information alone is not enough: 'if information was enough, librarians would be rich', so time-box learning, then go implement.

ideas.idea: In the age of AI, discernment is a survival skill: get smart enough to separate signal from noise rather than relying on experts.
ideas.detail: An AI-generated 'Chinese monk' video with 3 million views claiming a feng shui reason there is no such thing as a lazy woman was being shared by her smart, accomplished girlfriends as real; she DMed them that it was fake.

ideas.idea: Pretty privilege is a usable strategy: the same woman earns about 30% more with makeup than without, so 'do you want to be right or do you want to win?'
ideas.detail: Studies compare the same woman with and without makeup across service and professional industries, and being well groomed alone raises earnings; most men would do it for 30% more money. You decide your own line, but she will 'clown me up'.

ideas.idea: Mirroring people's speech and movements out of genuine curiosity builds connection and gets more done; insisting 'I am who I am, conform to me' does not get you far.
ideas.detail: Data shows people like you more when you mirror them non-creepily. The hosts identify leaning in and out of personas as one of Sanchez's superpowers; she prefers winning through connection.

ideas.idea: When negotiating salary, state your number and reasons in few words, then close with 'you can't blame a girl for asking', a smile and a shrug.
ideas.detail: Her sales mentor Rob taught her the line; it is disarming because the boss cannot get mad at it, and it is a negotiating superpower men cannot use. Women have negotiating advantages they largely leave unused.

ideas.idea: Every man you work with is one of three archetypes, the three Fs (father figure, friend, or guy who wants to sleep with you), and you adjust your ask to the category.
ideas.detail: With a father figure, ask for advice on how to negotiate so you end up on the same side of the table; with a friend, use a tongue-in-cheek 'would it be unreasonable if I asked' (a Chris Voss-ism) with a shrug; with the third type, play the tough card ('what are we doing here, are we going to lock this down?') rather than flirting.

ideas.idea: Prepare to win: a pound of pre-production is worth ten of post, and fear mostly bleeds away once you have prepared.
ideas.detail: The hosts add that women tend to over-prepare, and building the muscle means learning you need less preparation each time; 'prepare to win' also means expecting to win.

ideas.idea: Say fewer things: a high signal-to-noise ratio signals intelligence and earns respect, so replace 'I was kind of thinking maybe' with 'here is what we should do, here is why, A, B or C?'
ideas.detail: You become what you practice ('you don't get paid to be in the game, you get paid to practice; the game is the reward'). Deals are a zero-sum, immediate feedback loop on whether you communicated compellingly; if you are not doing deals, measure how often you get what you want out of life.

ideas.idea: A roll-up buys multiple small businesses in one category, centralizes HR, marketing, scheduling and software, gains supplier leverage, and earns multiple expansion, but it is not a beginner move.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Five rolled-up med spas can share one scheduling platform and negotiate Botox from Allergan down from, say, $5 to $3 a portion by buying for 100,000 patients instead of 1,000; the combined company gets valued at a higher multiple for being more professionalized and stable. Every problem of buying one business (culture, integration, compliance, 'why do these two locations hate each other') gets multiplied by five. Two of Cherie's Stanford professors rolled up traffic-cone logistics companies that serve highway construction. The hosts add that post-military MBAs are an archetype that succeeds as searchers because they want leadership again and can toggle between hourly blue-collar employees and the spreadsheets.
